dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?

Yes, good afternoon. Um, my name is Richard Sherman. I'm out on Rhode Island Avenue, four sixty-nine, up on the Hill. And I've got a, well, I want to put a deck off the back of the house, and I'm not sure what I have to do first.
Okay, Mr. Sherman, thanks. A deck, so a new one, not repairing an old one?
New. There's nothing back there now but a couple of concrete steps and some grass. So I'm wondering, does a deck need a permit? Or is that only for the big ones?

In general, a deck attached to the house does need a building permit. Small, low platforms sometimes are treated differently, so I'd want to know a bit more. About how big, and how high off the ground would it be?
Well, now, I was thinking twelve by fourteen. And high, I don't know, maybe three feet at the house end. The door sits up a ways from the yard. Is that high? I couldn't say what counts.
Three feet is high enough that I'd plan on a permit. And is it attached to the house, or would it stand on its own?
Attached, I think. Hm. Or is it better freestanding? I read something on the computer that said ledger board, and I didn't follow it at all.
That's the board that bolts the deck to the house wall. Attached is common, and it's one of the things the inspector looks at. Either way, you'd apply for the deck permit.
Okay. So that's the permit. And then does somebody have to come inspect it? Or do I just build it and send in the paper?

Yes, there's inspection. Usually someone looks at the footings before they're covered up, and then again when the framing's done, and a final at the end. The permit tells you exactly which ones are required.
Footings. Before they're covered. So I dig the holes, and then I call you, and I wait?
Right, you'd schedule the inspection once the holes are dug, before any concrete goes in. Don't pour until it's signed off.
Hm. Okay, so I pour after, not before. I had that backwards in my head. And is it me who applies, or the contractor? I might do some of it myself, and a fella might do the rest.
A homeowner can apply for work on their own house, or a licensed contractor can pull it. If a contractor does it, they'd usually take out the permit. Do you know yet who's building it?

Not yet. I was going to do the, ah, framing myself, maybe. Sorry, I'm running slow today. I'm on a vegetarian week, see, my daughter's idea, and I miss bacon something terrible. I think it's got my brain going soft.

[pause] Well, hang in there. So if you're doing it yourself, you can apply as the owner. You'd bring a simple drawing with the size, height, and how it's attached. Also, since you're on the Hill, it may need another look depending on whether your house is in a historic district.
Another look? From who? I thought the permit was the one thing.
It might be one thing, or it might be two. I'm not certain your block has that review for a rear deck, so I'll have someone confirm and let you know. Can I take your number?
Sure. It's four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-eight-seven.
Four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-eight-seven. And that's Richard Sherman, four sixty-nine Rhode Island Avenue?
That's it. So, just to say it back, I need a deck permit, I draw it up, I call for the footing inspection before I pour, and there may be a second review you're checking on.
That's right. Plus the framing and final inspections after the footings. Someone will call you back about the historic part.
All right. Thank you, Miss Chaudhry. I think I've got it, mostly. I'll write it down before I forget the order.
Sounds good. Have a good afternoon, Mr. Sherman.
You too. Bye now.
